explanation: Double-quoted strings interpolate variables and process escapes like \n, while single-quoted strings treat most escapes literally.
The null coalescing operator (??) uses isset()-like checks, so it returns the right operand without emitting undefined variable warnings when the left operand is unset or null.
The echo construct accepts multiple arguments and prints them consecutively with no separator, so 'a' and 'b' output as ab.
In PHP, print is a language construct that always evaluates to 1, so it can be used inside expressions such as $x = print "hi";.
The ?: operator returns its left operand when it is truthy, otherwise it returns the right operand.
As of PHP 8.0, the concatenation operator (.) has lower precedence than + and -, whereas previously they shared the same left-associative precedence.
The ** operator is right-associative in PHP, so 2 ** 3 ** 2 evaluates as 2 ** (3 ** 2) = 2 ** 9 = 512.
In PHP 8, concatenation (.) has higher precedence than addition, so 'sum: ' . 2 becomes the non-numeric string 'sum: 2', and adding 3 to a non-numeric string throws a TypeError.
The === operator compares arrays element by element in order, so different element orders make them unequal.
0 == false is a loose (non-strict) comparison and evaluates to true; a strict comparison would be ===.
In PHP 8, comparing a non-numeric string with a number converts the number to a string, so "abc" is compared with "0" and they are not equal (this was true only in PHP 7 and earlier).
In PHP, null loosely equals 0, "", and false, since each of those values casts null's comparison to a falsy equivalent.
Casting a string to int in PHP parses the leading numeric portion, so '42abc' becomes 42.
PHP converts the numeric string '5' to an integer before addition, so 5 + 5 equals 10.
Casting false to string in PHP yields an empty string "", not "0"; it is (string)(int)false that gives "0".
0.1 + 0.2 evaluates to 0.30000000000000004 due to floating-point precision, so it is not strictly equal to 0.3.
strrev() operates on bytes, so it can split multibyte UTF-8 characters and corrupt them.
str_contains() checks if the needle 'world' exists in the haystack 'Hello world', returning true.
str_pad() supports three pad types: STR_PAD_RIGHT (default), STR_PAD_LEFT, and STR_PAD_BOTH.
By default trim() strips all standard whitespace characters, including spaces, tabs (\t), newlines (\n), carriage returns (\r), null bytes (\0), and vertical tabs (\x0B).
strlen counts bytes, and UTF-8 'é' occupies 2 bytes, so 1+2+1+1+1 = 6.
A negative start position counts from the end of the string, so it returns the last three characters.
ucfirst() returns a new string and does not modify the original, since PHP strings are immutable value types.
Heredocs (<<<EOT) parse variables like double-quoted strings, while nowdocs (<<<'EOT') treat content literally with no interpolation.
sort() reindexes numeric keys, so the key-to-value association is not preserved (asort() does preserve it).
PHP casts numeric string keys (like '5') to integers when used as array keys.
in_array() uses loose comparison (==) by default; strict comparison requires passing true as the third argument.
array_filter() without a callback removes elements equal to false when compared loosely, i.e., empty/falsy values like false, null, 0, "", "0", and [].
By default array_slice() reindexes numeric keys; only string keys and the preserve_keys option keep original keys.
array_slice with offset 1 and length 2 returns elements from index 1 up to 2 items, giving [20, 30].
The + operator keeps the left operand's value for duplicate key 'a' and adds 'b' from the right, giving 2 elements.
PHP 8.1 added support for spreading arrays with string keys, later ones overriding earlier duplicates.
PHP permits mixing them, e.g. foo(...$args, a: 1) or foo(a: 1, ...$args) — and since PHP 8.1 the unpacked array may even contain string keys, which are treated as named arguments.
Anonymous functions create their own scope in PHP, so outer variables must be imported with the `use` keyword (only `$this` is inherited automatically).
func_num_args() returns the number of arguments actually passed to the function, which is 3.
With curly braces an arrow function has a block body that can contain multiple statements/expressions, though it returns undefined unless an explicit return is used.
PHP arrow functions automatically capture outer variables by value at creation time, not lazily by reference.
A static closure has no $this context and cannot bind or use $this, whereas a non-static closure captures $this automatically.
The closure captures $x by value when created, so it still holds 5 even after $x is reassigned to 7.
Without strict_types, PHP performs coercive type juggling and converts numeric strings like "5" to int.
Constructor property promotion was introduced in PHP 8.0, allowing parameters with visibility modifiers to automatically become class properties.
The `final` keyword on a method prevents it from being overridden in subclasses.
A final method cannot be overridden by any subclass, which is the main purpose of the final keyword on methods.
Private properties are only visible within the declaring class and cannot be accessed by subclasses.
Anonymous classes get the generated name 'class@anonymous', which is followed by a NUL byte and then the source file/line information, so only 'class@anonymous' precedes the NUL.
Private methods are not inherited in PHP, so a child class may declare a method with the same name and any visibility without conflict.
PHP also calls __get() when accessing inaccessible (protected or private) properties, not just non-existent ones.
PHP throws an Error (an Error subclass) when you attempt to modify an already initialized readonly property.
PHP interfaces can declare constants, and they are inherited by classes implementing the interface.
PHP's instanceof operator returns true if the given object is an instance of the specified class or implements the specified interface.
Since PHP 8.0, interfaces can declare static methods, though they must be implemented by implementing classes.
instanceof checks both class inheritance and interfaces (and traits), returning true if the object implements the given interface.
PHP interfaces cannot contain method bodies; default implementations belong to traits or abstract methods, so interface methods are always abstract.
Abstract methods in PHP can be declared with public or protected visibility (private abstract methods are not allowed), so a protected abstract method is valid.
Foo::cases() returns an array containing all defined enum cases, which are A, B, and C.
Traits may contain methods (including abstract and static) and properties (including static), but constants must be declared in a class or interface instead.
In PHP 7+, both Exception and Error implement the Throwable interface, making it their common ancestor.
TypeError extends Error, which is a sibling of Exception, so catch (Exception $e) does not catch it.
The @ error control operator only suppresses error messages (warnings, notices), not exceptions, which must be handled with try/catch.
intdiv() throws DivisionByZeroError (an ArithmeticError subclass) when dividing by zero, unlike the / operator which raises a warning and returns INF.
The finally block executes whether or not an exception was caught, as long as execution reaches it (e.g., no exit or fatal error intervenes).
An exception thrown in a finally block overrides any return value or exception from the try block, discarding it unless caught.
Casting any object to bool evaluates to true, since objects are always truthy.
Shutdown functions registered with register_shutdown_function() execute when the script ends, including when exit() or die() is called.
The use statement only creates an alias for the fully qualified name; the class file is actually loaded by the autoloader only when the class is first referenced, such as during instantiation.
PHP uses `use function Namespace\functionName;` to import a function, while `const` is for constants.
PSR-4 strips the App\ prefix and maps the remainder to the src/ directory, appending .php to the class name.
Composer's generated vendor/autoload.php uses spl_autoload_register() to register its autoloading functions, including the PSR-4/PSR-0 loaders.
The __NAMESPACE__ magic constant always returns the name of the current namespace as a string, or an empty string if none is defined.
An unqualified class name in new is resolved relative to the current namespace (and any use-import), not from the global root; a leading backslash is needed for the root.
PSR-4 strips the namespace prefix 'App\' and appends the remainder 'Model\User' to the base directory, giving src/Model/User.php.

Namespace import `use` declarations must appear at the outermost scope of a file (or inside a namespace block), so placing one inside a function body is a parse error, and imports are resolved at compile time for the whole file rather than per function.
In PHP, arrays are value types assigned by copy-on-write semantics, so they are copied on assignment unless explicitly passed or assigned by reference using the & operator.
PHP arrays use copy-on-assignment, so modifying $b does not affect $a.
In PHP, functions have their own scope, so variables defined outside must be declared with `global`, accessed via `$GLOBALS`, or passed as arguments to be visible inside.
$GLOBALS is a real reference to the global symbol table, so unsetting an element in it removes the variable globally, not just locally.
The function takes $n by reference and increments it, so 5 becomes 6.
By-value foreach iterates over a snapshot (copy-on-write), so modifications made to the array inside the loop are not seen in that pass — only foreach by reference sees the live array.
A static property belongs to the class itself and is shared among all instances, so changes in one object are visible in all others.
PHP casts boolean array keys to integers, so `true` becomes key 1 and is stored as an integer, not a bool.
Since PHP 7.0, generators may use `return $value;` and that value is retrievable via the `getReturn()` method once the generator has finished.
A generator is one-shot: calling rewind() on an already-run generator throws an Exception, so you must call the generator function again to get a fresh traversable instance.
yield from delegates the full iteration protocol to a nested generator or iterable, forwarding values both ways.
Since g() uses yield, calling it returns a Generator object rather than executing the body.
The generator yields from the array [1, 2, 3], so iterator_to_array produces an array of 3 elements.
SplStack is a stack implementation (LIFO — last in, first out), not a FIFO queue.
ArrayIterator is a built-in SPL class that wraps an array (or object) and implements the Iterator interface, allowing traversal with foreach or iterator methods.
ArrayObject implements IteratorAggregate, so it returns an Iterator via getIterator() and can be traversed with foreach.
password_hash() generates a random salt internally, and passing a salt explicitly was deprecated in PHP 7.4 and removed in PHP 8.0.
In PHP 8, PASSWORD_DEFAULT refers to bcrypt (currently 2y), not MD5.
password_verify returns true because the password matches the generated hash.
strip_tags() only removes HTML/PHP tags from a string and does nothing to make input safe for SQL queries; prepared statements with parameterized queries are the proper defense against SQL injection.
session_regenerate_id() generates a new session ID, which prevents an attacker from fixing a known session ID on the victim's login.
php_sapi_name() returns the name of the Server Application Programming Interface (SAPI) in use, such as 'cli' or 'fpm-fcgi'.
session_destroy() removes the data stored server-side for the session, but the session ID cookie must be deleted separately (e.g., with setcookie() for the session name with an expired time).
session_start() must be called before the $_SESSION superglobal becomes available and is populated with session data.
The array_find() function (along with array_find_key, array_any, and array_all) was added in PHP 8.4.
PHP 8.4 introduced property hooks, allowing get and set logic to be defined directly inside a property declaration.
PHP 8.4 introduced asymmetric visibility, allowing properties like `public private(set) string $name` to be publicly readable but only privately writable.
The #[\NoDiscard] attribute was introduced in PHP 8.5 to warn when a function's return value is ignored.
The pipe operator |> was accepted via RFC and introduced in PHP 8.5.
The clone-with syntax clone($obj, ['x' => 1]) was introduced in PHP 8.5.
PHP 7.3 added array_key_first() and array_key_last() (no core array_first()/array_last() exist), which is likely what the question refers to.
The RFC Partial Function Application v2 by Nicolas Grekas was adopted for PHP 8.6, since it was not part of the PHP 8.5 feature set.
The clamp_v2 RFC that adds the clamp() function was implemented for PHP 8.6 (the version current in development as of 2026-11-07).
No PHP RFC titled 'Context Managers v2' has been voted in and merged as of that date, so the statement is false.
The Bound-Erased Generic Types generics RFC was put to a vote in 2026 and failed to achieve the required support, so it was rejected.
No RFC making ZTS (thread-safe builds) the default has been accepted; it remains a non-default, opt-in build option.
PHP has never natively supported generics; as of PHP 8.5 they remain unsupported, with only static analyzers like Psalm and PHPStan providing generic-style typing.
PHP 8.5.0 was released in November 2025, so it remains the latest stable release as of 2026-11-07, with PHP 8.6's GA scheduled for later in November 2026.
The PHP 6 project focused on Unicode support and was cancelled, so the version numbering jumped from 5.6 to 7.0.
The #[\Deprecated] attribute RFC was accepted and introduced in PHP 8.4 to allow deprecating functions, methods, and constants.
In clean and onion architecture, inner layers are independent of outer ones, so all dependencies point inward toward the core/domain.
Domain entities should remain framework- and infrastructure-agnostic, depending only on the language and possibly the standard library.
Controllers and Twig templates belong to the presentation (interface) layer; only the use cases and entities themselves belong to the business-logic layer.
In onion architecture the innermost layer is the Entities (domain model/business entities) layer, containing core enterprise business rules.
Tools like Deptrac statically analyze the code and exit with an error when a call crosses a forbidden layer boundary.
A use case must stay framework- and transport-agnostic, so it should take a plain input DTO and depend on domain repository interfaces rather than an HTTP Request or an EntityManager.
A repository exposes collections of aggregates/entities through an interface, abstracting the underlying persistence mechanism.

In clean architecture the dependency rule keeps domain and use-case layers independent of persistence details, so only the infrastructure/adapter layer implementing the repository interfaces must change when swapping databases.
In DDD, an aggregate is a cluster of domain objects treated as a single unit with a root entity, not a database table mapping.
In Domain-Driven Design, a Value Object has no identity and is defined solely by its immutable attributes, so equality is based on field values.
In DDD, the aggregate root is the single entry point through which all external access and modifications of the aggregate's invariants must be performed.
In Domain-Driven Design, repositories manage aggregate roots to preserve invariants, rather than individual entities.
In Domain-Driven Design, the ubiquitous language is a common language shared by developers and domain experts throughout the project.

In Domain-Driven Design, a bounded context is the boundary inside which a model and its ubiquitous language keep a consistent meaning, while outside it the same terms are interpreted by other models/contexts.
DDD favors a rich domain model where business logic and invariants live in the domain objects themselves, not in anemic get/set DTOs manipulated by services.
In Domain-Driven Design, a bounded context defines a boundary within which a domain model is consistent, so the same term can be represented by different classes or meanings in different contexts.
By default, Symfony services are only instantiated when they are first requested from the container (though the optional 'lazy: true' flag adds an additional proxy layer).
The `debug:router` command lists all registered routes (with alias `router:debug`).
Autowiring automatically resolves constructor dependencies by type-hint, so most services do not need manual declaration.
Twig compiles each template into a PHP class and writes it to a cache file so it doesn't need to be recompiled on every request.
In dev, Symfony checks for file changes on each request but only recompiles/dumps the container when tracked files have actually changed.
APP_ENV is the environment variable Symfony uses to select the active environment such as dev or prod.
Symfony controllers must be public because the routing/action dispatcher invokes them from outside the class, so private or protected methods cannot be called.

Event subscribers are just regular listeners registered with default priority 0, so their execution order relative to other listeners depends on priority and registration order, not on being subscribers.
Symfony Security's Guard authenticator system was deprecated in 5.4 and removed in 6.0, where the Authenticator-based system is the only supported approach.
The IsGranted attribute from Symfony Security denies access with a 403 unless the user has the given role or permission.
Symfony's Security Voter component returns a decision for isGranted() calls with an attribute and an object, such as isGranted('EDIT', $post).
Since Symfony 7.0 the legacy doctrine/annotations-based mapping was removed, so validation constraints must be declared as PHP attributes (or in XML/YAML).
Symfony forms include and automatically validate a CSRF token on submission unless explicitly disabled.
Symfony always performs server-side validation regardless of any client-side checks, since HTML5 validation can be bypassed.
The Symfony MakerBundle command 'make:form' interactively generates a FormType class.
Symfony calls eraseCredentials() after authentication, removing the plain password before the user object is serialized into the session.
With Symfony Flex, each bundle's or topic's configuration is conventionally placed in its own file under config/packages/ (e.g., config/packages/twig.yaml).
This is a common convention where safe development defaults are versioned in .env while sensitive overrides in .env.local are excluded via .gitignore.
The debug:container command lists all registered services and their aliases in the Symfony container.
setParameter() is a public method on the Container class, so it can be called from a controller and the new value is visible for the rest of the request.
Since Symfony 3.4, services are private by default and must be explicitly marked public to be fetched directly from the container.
Most bundles ship with sensible default configuration and work without a config file.
Symfony resolves %env(VAR)% placeholders in configuration files like services.yaml to environment variable values at runtime.
APP_DEBUG controls the debug mode, enabling the Symfony profiler and Twig debug features.
Symfony Messenger supports routing a single message to multiple handlers, each of which can process it independently.
The sync transport handles the message immediately in the same process rather than queueing it for a worker.
The messenger:consume console command starts a worker that consumes and processes messages from the configured transport.
In Symfony Messenger, the retry_strategy (max_retries, delay, multiplier, jitter) is set under the options of each individual transport in config/packages/messenger.yaml.
Symfony Messenger's default transport serializer (the SerializerMessageDecoding class) uses the JSON format by default.
The Symfony Scheduler component generates messages at defined times and sends them to a Messenger transport for dispatching.
The built-in 'doctrine' Messenger transport persists messages in database tables through Doctrine DBAL.
Symfony Messenger allows registering custom middleware in the bus configuration with a priority, enabling them to run before or after the built-in middleware.
Symfony follows a release policy of new major versions every two years and minor versions every six months, released in May and November.
Symfony 8 requires PHP 8.4 or higher as its minimum supported version.
Symfony 7.0 removed support for doctrine/annotations-based docblocks for routing and validation, requiring PHP attributes instead.
AssetMapper uses importmap.php to map and serve CSS/JS assets natively without needing Node.js or bundlers like Webpack.
Symfony 6.4 is a Long-Term Support (LTS) release, offering 3 years of bug fixes and 4 years of security fixes.
Symfony removes deprecated code in the next major version, since major releases are allowed to break backward compatibility.
Symfony provides UPGRADE.md (or UPGRADE files) in its repository that document breaking changes and migration steps for each major version.
Symfony's AssetMapper component maps and bundles static assets and manages the importmap (via its ImportMapManager) directly in PHP, with no Node.js or Webpack required.
Symfony 8.2 is scheduled for late November 2026, so it would not yet be released on 2026-11-07.
Symfony majors ship every two years in November (8.0 in Nov 2025), so minor 8.1 lands May 2026 and 8.2 follows in November 2026 on the six-month cycle.
Following Symfony's twice-yearly release cycle, 8.2 is the version after 8.1.
8.2 is only a minor release on the 8.x branch, not a major release, so it follows Symfony's backward compatibility promise and does not require rewriting applications for new APIs.
PHP maintains backward compatibility within a major release series, so moving from 8.1 to 8.2 should not break existing code (only new deprecations may be introduced).
Symfony follows a two-year major release cycle, so the 8.x branch runs from 8.0 (Nov 2025) to 8.4 (Nov 2027), the final minor released alongside the new 9.0 major.
Symfony only raises its minimum PHP version in major releases, so Symfony 8.2 (a minor release) would not require PHP 8.5; Symfony 8.0 is expected to require PHP 8.4.
Symfony's deprecation policy keeps code deprecated in a major version branch (like 8.x) until the next major version (9.0), so they are not removed any earlier than 9.0.
Twig's {{ }} only evaluates Twig expressions and filters, not arbitrary PHP code, for security reasons.
Since Twig 2.x, autoescaping is enabled by default using the HTML escaping strategy.
The |e filter (alias of escape) converts special characters to their HTML entities by default, with strategy options like js, css, url, or html for other contexts.
The format_number filter from twig/intl-extra formats a number according to a given locale using ICU/NumberFormatter.
The |raw filter in Twig marks the value as safe HTML, disabling automatic escaping.
In Twig, {{ ... }} outputs an expression's value while {% ... %} is used for control structures like if, for, and set.
Twig lets you declare variables with the set tag (e.g. {% set foo = 'bar' %}), so values don't only come from the controller.
The dump() Twig function outputs the debug structure of a variable, similar to var_dump or Symfony's VarDumper.
Bootstrap is a front-end CSS/JavaScript toolkit providing ready-made UI components like grids, buttons, and modals, not a single-page application framework.
The .container class provides a responsive fixed-width container whose max-width changes at each Bootstrap breakpoint, unlike .container-fluid which is always 100% wide.
Bootstrap's grid has 12 columns, and Bootstrap 4+ uses flexbox rather than floats.
Bootstrap 5 defines exactly those five named breakpoints (sm 576px, md 768px, lg 992px, xl 1200px, xxl 1400px), with the base tier having no infix.
In Bootstrap, spacing utilities multiply the $spacer variable (default 1rem) by the utility's numeric suffix, so .mt-3 = 3 × $spacer.
Bootstrap 5 uses data-bs-toggle (e.g., data-bs-toggle="dropdown") to activate interactive components on an element.
Bootstrap 5 removed the jQuery dependency and its components are implemented in vanilla JavaScript.
Bootstrap 5.3 enables dark mode via the data-bs-theme="dark" attribute on an element, not a .dark class.
Doctrine does not create tables automatically; you must use a schema tool or run schema:create/update commands explicitly.
EntityManager::persist() marks a new entity as managed and scheduled for insertion, with SQL executed only on flush().
The merge() method was removed in Doctrine ORM 3.0 (deprecated in 2.x), so it no longer exists.
DQL is an object-oriented query language that operates on entities and their properties rather than database tables and columns.
Repository find methods based on Eloquent return null when no matching record is found.
Doctrine does not automatically call flush() at the end of a request; it must be called explicitly in your code.
Doctrine's Unit of Work detects dirty state on managed entities during flush(), so no explicit persist() is needed for updates.
remove() only marks the entity for deletion; the SQL DELETE is executed when flush() is called.
MVCC gives readers and writers non-blocking access, so they do not block each other (only conflicting writers block each other).
The EXPLAIN command returns the query execution plan without actually running the query.
SERIAL is a legacy shorthand that creates a sequence default value, whereas GENERATED ... AS IDENTITY is the SQL-standard identity column mechanism, so they are similar but not identical.
In PostgreSQL, NULL values are considered distinct, so a UNIQUE constraint allows multiple rows with NULL by default.
PostgreSQL's string_agg() joins string values with a specified delimiter (e.g., string_agg(name, ', ')).
Plain VACUUM only marks dead-tuple space as reusable within the table; only VACUUM FULL (which rewrites the table) actually returns disk space to the OS.
The PARTITION BY clause in a window function divides the result set into partitions, and the window function is computed separately over each partition.
READ COMMITTED only guarantees each statement sees the latest committed data, so a row can change between statements (non-repeatable reads occur); REPEATABLE READ is what prevents them.
PostgreSQL runs each statement in its own implicit transaction when no explicit BEGIN block is active, committing automatically on success.
COMMIT ends the current transaction and permanently saves all changes made within it.
UPDATE and DELETE statements with a WHERE clause on an indexed column can locate matching rows faster, just like SELECT does.
PostgreSQL supports SAVEPOINT (and RELEASE SAVEPOINT / ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT) to roll back only part of a transaction.
EXPLAIN ANALYZE executes the query and reports actual row counts and timing, unlike plain EXPLAIN which only shows the plan.
pgvector adds the vector data type and indexes (IVFFlat, HNSW) for similarity/embedding search in PostgreSQL.
A partial index includes only rows matching the WHERE condition, making it smaller and faster to maintain.
PostgreSQL implements SERIALIZABLE using Serializable Snapshot Isolation (SSI), which tracks read/write dependencies rather than locking read rows.
HTTP 201 Created is returned when a request has been fulfilled and has resulted in one or more new resources being created.
204 No Content signals a successful request with no response body, commonly used after DELETE.
The HTTP specification defines DELETE as idempotent because repeating it leaves the resource in the same state (gone), even if the second response differs.
The Access-Control-Allow-Origin response header is sent by the server, not the client, to indicate which origins are permitted to access the resource.
HTTP status 429 Too Many Requests indicates the client has exceeded the server's rate limit.
4xx codes indicate client errors while 5xx codes indicate server-side errors, so the statement is reversed.
The Content-Type header specifies the MIME type of the body in both HTTP requests and responses.
RFC 5789 explicitly states that PATCH is not idempotent (nor safe), whereas PUT is defined as idempotent.
Plain == can leak comparison timing and is vulnerable to timing attacks, so hash_equals() should be used instead.
CSRF tokens are generated server-side, tied to the user's session, and validated by the server before processing unsafe requests.
The Content-Security-Policy HTTP response header is used to enable and configure a site's CSP policy.

OAuth 2.0 is an authorization framework, not an authentication protocol; access tokens grant access to resources rather than definitively identifying the user (OpenID Connect is built on OAuth 2.0 for authentication).
XSS is prevented primarily by escaping/encoding output when rendering data, not merely by validating input before storing it.
The authorization code (code parameter) is returned to the redirect_uri and then exchanged for an access token at the token endpoint.
Refresh tokens are long-lived credentials used to obtain new short-lived access tokens without requiring re-authentication.
Salts are stored alongside the hash and are not secret; their purpose is to defeat precomputed rainbow tables, while verification simply uses the stored salt with the input password.
PHPUnit only executes test methods in classes that extend PHPUnit\Framework\TestCase (or subclasses like TestCase).
In PHPUnit, setUp() runs before each individual test, while setUpBeforeClass() runs once before all tests in the class.
A data provider lets a test run with multiple sets of arguments, each iteration running the test once.
expectException() is called on the test case (e.g., $this->expectException(MyException::class);) to assert that the code under test throws that exception class.
It's the reverse: mocks verify method calls/interactions, while stubs provide canned return values.
PHPUnit 10 introduced PHP attributes and deprecated doc-comment metadata like @dataProvider in favor of #[DataProvider].
PHPUnit supports the @depends annotation, which lets one test receive the return value of another.
PHPUnit's --order-by=random option randomizes the order in which tests are executed.
